title: Voter Roll Purges and Mass Disenfranchisement - Federal Access to State Registration Databases
description_short: Voter Roll Purges and Mass Disenfranchisement - Federal Access to State Registration Databases
description_medium: Project 2025-related analyses warn that changes to federal voting-rights enforcement could weaken protections, but the supplied materials do not document a federal requirement that states provide voter-registration or DMV data to DHS in exchange for grant funding. They also do not show coordinated voter purges under such a condition.
description_long: The supplied materials concern Project 2025 and potential changes to federal voting-rights enforcement. Common Cause warns that reducing the Justice Department Civil Rights Division’s capacity could weaken enforcement of the Voting Rights Act and National Voter Registration Act. That concern is distinct from the entry’s more specific claim that the Trump administration conditioned Department of Homeland Security grants on states providing voter-registration and motor-vehicle records, then used the data to direct mass purges. The packet does not identify a grant condition, directive, participating states, database transfers or resulting registration removals. It therefore does not establish that the alleged federal data-sharing program or coordinated purge campaign occurred. The issue could be documented with the relevant DHS grant terms or directive and state records showing participation and effects. Until those are available, the entry should be framed around proposed changes to voting-rights enforcement rather than as a completed federal voter-suppression operation.

preserved_fields.title: Voter Roll Purges and Mass Disenfranchisement - Federal Access to State Registration Databases
preserved_fields.description_short: Voter Roll Purges and Mass Disenfranchisement - Federal Access to State Registration Databases

notes: Missing context: DHS grant language or directive requiring state voter/DMV data, jurisdictions that complied, and records showing database use or voter removals. Proposed correction: describe documented Project 2025 voting-rights proposals unless those implementation records are identified.

title: Most Americans Said Trump's Iran War Wasn't Going Well
description_short: Most Americans Said Trump's Iran War Wasn't Going Well
description_medium: A CBS News/YouGov poll fielded March 17–20, 2026, found that most Americans thought the Iran conflict was not going well and called it a war of choice rather than necessity. Respondents wanted the fighting to end quickly, were concerned about rising gas prices and did not expect the war to strengthen the economy. Republican and MAGA voters remained more supportive of Trump and the campaign.
description_long: CBS News and YouGov surveyed 3,335 U.S. adults from March 17 through 20, 2026, with a reported margin of error of 2.1 percentage points. The poll found that most respondents said the Iran conflict was not going well, and most described it as a war of choice rather than necessity. Many said the administration had not clearly explained its goals; respondents also wanted the conflict to end quickly and linked it to higher gasoline prices and concern about the economy. Most did not expect the war to improve the U.S. economy, and only a little more than one-third thought it would make the country safer in the long term. Views were divided by party: the president’s Republican base, particularly MAGA voters, expressed stronger support for the military action and confidence in Trump, while disapproval was more common among Democrats and independents. The survey records public opinion at a particular point during the conflict; it does not measure battlefield outcomes or establish what policy course the administration would take next. The supplied report gives the survey period and methodology but the available article text does not state every response percentage.

preserved_fields.title: Most Americans Said Trump's Iran War Wasn't Going Well
preserved_fields.description_short: Most Americans Said Trump's Iran War Wasn't Going Well

notes: CBS/YouGov reports a nationally representative sample of 3,335 adults, interviewed March 17–20, with a ±2.1-point margin of error. The accessible article text summarizes findings but does not state every response percentage.

title: Trump's Deportation Machine Was So Warehousing-Obsessed DHS Had to Pause New Immigrant Holding Deals
description_short: Trump's Deportation Machine Was So Warehousing-Obsessed DHS Had to Pause New Immigrant Holding Deals
description_medium: DHS paused purchases of additional warehouses for immigrant detention while reviewing contracts signed under former secretary Kristi Noem. The Associated Press reported that 11 warehouses had already been bought for $1.074 billion and that the department was scrutinizing those purchases too. The pause followed Markwayne Mullin’s arrival as DHS secretary; it did not end the broader detention expansion.
description_long: The Associated Press reported on April 1, 2026, that the Department of Homeland Security had paused purchases of additional warehouses intended for immigrant detention while reviewing contracts signed under former secretary Kristi Noem. A senior department official said the review also covered purchases already completed. DHS had spent a combined $1.074 billion to buy 11 warehouses in eight states, and the department had inherited a $38.3 billion plan to expand detention capacity to 92,000 beds through large detention centers and regional processing sites. The purchases drew local opposition over the facilities’ presence and possible demands on water and sewer systems. Lawsuits were pending in three states, while some proposed deals had collapsed when owners declined to sell. At least one planned facility had been scaled back: the Surprise, Arizona, site was limited to 542 occupied beds, down from an initial 1,500-bed proposal, according to the city’s mayor. The pause occurred shortly after Markwayne Mullin became DHS secretary. It concerned new acquisitions and contract review; it did not establish that the existing warehouses would close or that the administration had abandoned its detention-expansion plans.

preserved_fields.title: Trump's Deportation Machine Was So Warehousing-Obsessed DHS Had to Pause New Immigrant Holding Deals
preserved_fields.description_short: Trump's Deportation Machine Was So Warehousing-Obsessed DHS Had to Pause New Immigrant Holding Deals

notes: The report documents a purchase pause and contract review, not a termination of the broader detention plan or a finding that the contracts were unlawful.

title: Trump's Hormuz Mess Was Still Showing Up at the Gas Pump
description_short: Trump's Hormuz Mess Was Still Showing Up at the Gas Pump
description_medium: An April 17 report linked traffic concerns and uncertainty in the Persian Gulf to slower declines in gasoline prices after the Strait of Hormuz reopened to commercial shipping. The supplied material gives no April price figure or shipping data. A later July report describes a different period and cannot establish the conditions or prices in this entry’s timeframe.
description_long: The entry concerns the possible effect of shipping uncertainty in the Persian Gulf on gasoline prices after the Strait of Hormuz reopened to commercial traffic. The linked Associated Press headline says traffic and trepidation could keep prices from dropping quickly, but the article page was not accessible for review. The other linked report is dated July 16 and concerns a later period of U.S.–Iran tension, including a separate Strait closure and higher fuel prices. It cannot supply the April 17 price data or explain the shipping conditions described in the AP headline. The material provided here does not establish what drivers were paying, how long the Strait had been open, the volume of commercial traffic or how much any uncertainty contributed to prices. The headline also assigns the economic effect to Trump, but the available facts do not isolate that causal link. A dated price series and contemporaneous shipping details are needed to describe the event’s scale and attribution accurately.

preserved_fields.title: Trump's Hormuz Mess Was Still Showing Up at the Gas Pump
preserved_fields.description_short: Trump's Hormuz Mess Was Still Showing Up at the Gas Pump

notes: Missing context: contemporaneous April 17 gasoline prices, the Strait’s reopening timeline and shipping data, and the AP report’s evidence connecting those conditions to prices. The later Guardian article is from July and describes a distinct period. Proposed correction: state the documented price and shipping conditions without attributing them to Trump unless the report supports that link.

title: Trump Claimed Iranians Welcomed US Infrastructure Strikes Without Proof
description_short: Trump Claimed Iranians Welcomed US Infrastructure Strikes Without Proof
description_medium: At a White House press conference on April 6, Trump said U.S. intelligence had intercepted Iranians near bombing sites urging U.S. forces to keep striking, but the report provided no evidence for that claim. He argued that civilians would accept losing power and basic services to escape Iran’s government, as he threatened attacks on energy facilities and bridges if the Strait of Hormuz remained closed.
description_long: The Guardian reported that Trump claimed on April 6 that Iranian civilians welcomed U.S. attacks on their country’s infrastructure. At a White House press conference, he said intercepted communications showed people near active bombing sites urging U.S. forces to continue, but the article offered no supporting evidence for those alleged intercepts. Trump argued that civilians would be willing to lose electricity and other services in pursuit of freedom from Iran’s government. He invoked the 2022 “Woman, Life, Freedom” protests to describe the repression Iranians faced and dismissed concerns that striking infrastructure would punish civilians. He also threatened strikes on energy facilities and bridges if Iran did not reopen the Strait of Hormuz by an 8 p.m. Tuesday deadline. Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth said the day’s attacks would be the largest volume since the operation began. Democratic lawmakers and Iran’s U.N. mission warned that attacks on civilian infrastructure could violate the laws of war; those were objections to the threatened targets, not a court finding about a completed strike. The report documents Trump’s assertion and threat, but not evidence that civilians welcomed the proposed attacks.
organization_tags: Iranian Mission to the United Nations

preserved_fields.title: Trump Claimed Iranians Welcomed US Infrastructure Strikes Without Proof
preserved_fields.description_short: Trump Claimed Iranians Welcomed US Infrastructure Strikes Without Proof

notes: The source reports Trump’s account of intercepted communications but supplies no evidence for it. The threat to strike infrastructure is distinct from proof that those strikes occurred.

title: Trump Promised Peace, but Dearborn Got Another Reminder of the Lie
description_short: Trump Promised Peace, but Dearborn Got Another Reminder of the Lie
description_medium: The linked report is titled “Trump promised peace in the Middle East. In Dearborn, Michigan, it feels farther away.” The supplied synopsis identifies Dearborn’s large Arab American community but does not say which local events or effects residents described, or quote the promise being compared with them.
description_long: The linked report frames the distance between Trump’s Middle East peace promise and how the situation feels in Dearborn, Michigan, which has a large Arab American community. The supplied record does not identify the particular events residents were reacting to, describe effects on families or local organizations, or quote the promise and its date. The article links in the packet returned HTTP 404 and 403, so the headline and short synopsis do not provide enough evidence for a fuller account. Without a chronology and specific community examples, the entry cannot explain what changed in Dearborn or attribute those changes to a particular administration decision. A useful revision needs the report’s account of the local consequences and the exact promise it contrasts with them. Until then, the title’s claim that residents received a reminder of a “lie” is an interpretation rather than an established description of a specific event.

preserved_fields.title: Trump Promised Peace, but Dearborn Got Another Reminder of the Lie
preserved_fields.description_short: Trump Promised Peace, but Dearborn Got Another Reminder of the Lie

notes: Missing context: the specific local events and effects described by residents, the exact Trump peace commitment and its date, and the report’s chronology linking the two. Both supplied story pages were inaccessible (ABC 404; AP 403). Proposed correction: describe the documented community experience and quote the promise before assigning causation or calling it a lie.

title: Trump: Roy Cohn stars in Joseph McCarthy's investigation, invents McCarthyism
description_short: Trump: Roy Cohn stars in Joseph McCarthy's investigation, invents McCarthyism
description_medium: In 1953, Senator Joseph McCarthy hired Roy Cohn as chief counsel to the Senate Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations. McCarthy relied on Cohn for contacts, information, ideas and political advice during the investigations that became emblematic of the era’s Red Scare. The appointment is documented; the source does not establish that Cohn alone invented McCarthyism.
description_long: Senator Joseph McCarthy hired Roy Cohn in 1953 as chief counsel to the Senate Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations. PBS’s account says McCarthy relied heavily on Cohn for contacts, information, ideas and political advice. The committee’s investigations became among the best-known episodes of the 1950s Red Scare, when allegations of communist influence in government and public life drew national attention. Cohn’s appointment placed him in a central legal and political role in McCarthy’s investigations, but the available material does not support the title’s claim that he “invented McCarthyism.” The term refers to a broader political phenomenon associated with McCarthy and the period, and a chief-counsel appointment alone cannot establish individual authorship of it. The record documents Cohn’s position and his influence within McCarthy’s operation; it does not identify a particular investigation or testimony as the moment the wider movement began. The entry is therefore best read as a snapshot of Cohn’s role in the Senate investigations, not as proof that one person originated the entire political campaign.
organization_tags: U.S. Senate Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations

preserved_fields.title: Trump: Roy Cohn stars in Joseph McCarthy's investigation, invents McCarthyism
preserved_fields.description_short: Trump: Roy Cohn stars in Joseph McCarthy's investigation, invents McCarthyism

title: Trump: Czech Intelligence: Donald Trump is tax exempt until 2007
description_short: Trump: Czech Intelligence: Donald Trump is tax exempt until 2007
description_medium: A 1977 Czechoslovak intelligence informant described Donald Trump as “completely tax-exempt for the next 30 years,” according to a secret-service file later reported by The Guardian. The report also attributes to a separate file an account of Trump and Ivana’s prenuptial agreement. These are claims recorded by informants, not proof of Trump’s actual tax status or the agreement’s terms.
description_long: The Guardian reported that communist-era Czechoslovak intelligence, the StB, monitored Donald Trump and his then-wife Ivana during the 1970s and 1980s. A 1977 report by an informant using the cover name “Lubos” described Trump’s businesses as safe because they received state commissions and said he was “completely tax-exempt for the next 30 years.” The article presents that wording as a claim in an intelligence file, not as a verified account of Trump’s tax status. A separate file reportedly summarized a prenuptial agreement under which Trump would pay Ivana $1 million if the marriage ended. The Guardian also notes that the informant did not explain the asserted tax exemption and that later tax records reported by The New York Times concerned a different matter: a $916 million loss on Trump’s 1995 return that could have reduced income-tax liability for up to 18 years. The Czech file therefore documents what an informant told the StB, not independent proof of an exemption or a complete record of the couple’s financial arrangements. Its claims should remain attributed to the file and its source.

preserved_fields.title: Trump: Czech Intelligence: Donald Trump is tax exempt until 2007
preserved_fields.description_short: Trump: Czech Intelligence: Donald Trump is tax exempt until 2007

notes: The “tax-exempt” statement is attributed to an StB informant and is not verified as Trump’s actual tax status. The linked reporting says the intelligence file did not explain the basis for the claim.
